topics.name: President pro tempore of the Senate
topics.kicker: Highest-ranking senator · Third in line for the presidency
topics.briefing: The Constitution makes the vice president the President of the Senate, but vice presidents are rarely there, so senators choose one of their own members to preside “for the time being,” which is what pro tempore means in Latin. By custom, the job goes to the longest-serving senator of the majority party, and it puts its holder third in line for the presidency. In 2023, Patty Murray of Washington became the first woman to hold it.
topics.answerHtml: President pro tempore of the Senate (or President pro tem; prompt on pro tempore or presiding officer; do not accept “President of the Senate,” “Vice President,” or “Speaker of the House”)
accept: president pro tempore of the senate
president pro tempore of the us senate
president pro tempore of the united states senate
president pro tem of the senate
reject: vice president of the united states
speaker of the house of representatives

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Article I, Section 3 of the Constitution says the Senate shall choose this officer “in the Absence of the Vice President, or when he shall exercise the Office of President of the United States.” Senators elect one of their own members to this post, and by custom they pick the longest-serving member of the majority party.
tossups.r: Its name includes a Latin phrase meaning “for the time being.” For 10 points, name this Senate office, third in the presidential line of succession.

tossups.p: Under the Presidential Succession Act of 1792, the holder of this office came next in line for the presidency after the vice president, even ahead of the Speaker of the House. An 1886 law dropped both of those congressional leaders from the line of succession, but a 1947 law brought them back.
tossups.r: That law placed this office right after the Speaker. For 10 points, name this Senate office, third in line for the presidency.

tossups.p: In 1868, Benjamin Wade of Ohio held this office, so he would have become president if the Senate had removed Andrew Johnson, who had no vice president. Some historians think a few senators voted to acquit Johnson partly because they did not want Wade, a Radical Republican, in the White House.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this office, whose holder presides over the Senate when the vice president is absent.

tossups.p: A popular legend says that David Rice Atchison of Missouri, who held this office, was president for one day in 1849, because Zachary Taylor would not take the oath of office on a Sunday. Historians reject that story, partly because Atchison never took the presidential oath himself.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this office, usually given to the longest-serving senator of the majority party.

tossups.p: In April 1789, the Senate chose John Langdon of New Hampshire as the first person to hold this office, so that he could count the electoral votes from the first presidential election before the vice president took office.
tossups.r: Its holder presides over the Senate whenever the vice president is away. For 10 points, name this office, third in line for the presidency.

tossups.p: Daniel Inouye [“in-NOH-ay”] of Hawaii, a World War II Medal of Honor recipient, became the first Asian American to hold this office in 2010. He took over from Robert Byrd of West Virginia, the longest-serving senator in history, who held this post until he died.
tossups.r: It usually goes to the majority party’s most senior senator. For 10 points, name this Senate office, third in line for the presidency.

tossups.p: Because the Chief Justice presides only when a sitting president is on trial, Patrick Leahy of Vermont presided over the 2021 Senate impeachment trial of Donald Trump, who had already left office, while holding this office. Leahy held this post twice, the second time until he retired in 2023.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this office, whose holder presides over the Senate when the vice president is absent.

tossups.p: In 2001, the Senate created an honorary “emeritus” version of this office for Strom Thurmond of South Carolina, who had held this office for much of the 1980s and 1990s. Thurmond kept serving in the Senate until he was 100 years old.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this office, usually held by the most senior senator of the majority party.

tossups.p: Arthur Vandenberg of Michigan held this office when he sponsored a 1948 resolution that paved the way for the NATO alliance. A former isolationist, Vandenberg also worked with President Harry Truman to win Senate support for the Marshall Plan.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this office, whose holder presides over the Senate when the vice president is absent.

tossups.p: In January 2025, Chuck Grassley of Iowa was elected to this office at the age of 91, returning to a post he had held from 2019 to 2021. He took over from Patty Murray of Washington, who in 2023 had become the first woman to hold it.
tossups.r: This office usually goes to the longest-serving senator of the majority party. For 10 points, name this office, third in line for the presidency.

tossups.p: Robert Byrd, who held this office several times, wrote a four-volume history of the Senate and often carried a copy of the Constitution in his pocket. Byrd, a West Virginian who became the longest-serving senator in history, last held this office from 2007 until his death in 2010.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this office, whose holder presides over the Senate when the vice president is away.

tossups.p: Holders of this office rarely preside over the Senate’s daily sessions in person; instead, junior senators of the majority party take turns holding the gavel. Unlike the vice president, the holder of this office may vote on any bill, not only to break ties.
tossups.r: This office’s name includes a Latin phrase meaning “for the time being.” For 10 points, name this office, third in line for the presidency.

tossups.p: In 1977, the Senate created a “deputy” version of this office for Hubert Humphrey, a former vice president who had failed to win the post of majority leader. Humphrey held that new post until his death in January 1978.
tossups.r: Under a 1947 law, the holder of the main office comes right after the Speaker in the line of succession. For 10 points, name this Senate office.

tossups.p: Thomas Ferry of Michigan held this office when he presided over the count of electoral votes in the disputed election of 1876, because Vice President Henry Wilson had died in office. In March 1877, Ferry announced that Rutherford B. Hayes had won by a single electoral vote.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this office, held by the senator who presides over the Senate when the vice president is absent.

tossups.p: Orrin Hatch of Utah held this office from 2015 to 2019, between Patrick Leahy and Chuck Grassley. Because the post goes to the most senior senator of whichever party holds a majority, it usually changes hands when control of the Senate flips.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this office, third in line for the presidency after the vice president and the Speaker of the House.

clues.t: Third in the presidential line of succession, after the vice president and the Speaker of the House
Presides over the Senate when the vice president, the official President of the Senate, is absent
clues.rabbit: Vice President of the United States

trap.title: Which presiding officer?
trap.body: The Constitution makes the vice president the “President of the Senate,” so that answer is wrong here even though it sounds almost the same. The Senate majority leader, who runs the Senate’s day-to-day business, is a different job, and the Speaker of the House leads the House and comes just ahead of this office in the line of succession. Famous holders like Robert Byrd or Patty Murray can tempt you to buzz with a name when the question wants the office.
trap.fix: Listen for “for the time being,” “when the vice president is absent,” or “longest-serving senator of the majority party.” “Third in line” means the President pro tempore; “second in line” means the Speaker; “first in line” or “breaks ties” means the vice president.
trap.line: Real answer line: President pro tempore of the Senate (or President pro tem; prompt on pro tempore or presiding officer; do not accept “President of the Senate,” “Vice President,” or “Speaker of the House”)

topics.name: Republic of Texas
topics.kicker: Independent nation from 1836 to 1845 · Joined the U.S. as the 28th state
topics.briefing: For almost ten years, Texas was its own country, with its own president, army, navy, money, and flag. After winning independence from Mexico at San Jacinto in 1836, the Republic of Texas chose Sam Houston as its first elected president and later moved its capital from the young town of Houston to a new frontier city named Austin. In 1845, the United States annexed it as the 28th state, which helped start the Mexican-American War.
topics.answerHtml: Republic of Texas (or Texas Republic or Lone Star Republic; prompt on Texas)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In February 1846, this nation’s last president, Anson Jones, lowered its flag at a ceremony and declared that the nation was “no more.” Jones is sometimes called the “Architect of Annexation” for helping it join a much larger country.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this independent nation, led earlier by Sam Houston, that existed from 1836 until the United States annexed it.

tossups.p: In 1839, a commission picked a frontier village called Waterloo on the Colorado River as the site of a new capital, a spot favored by this nation’s second president, Mirabeau Lamar [“MEER-uh-boh luh-MAR”]. Lamar also pushed to set aside public land to pay for schools and universities.
tossups.r: The new capital was named for Stephen F. Austin. For 10 points, name this nation that existed from 1836 to 1845.

tossups.p: In December 1842, Angelina Eberly fired a cannon to stop men sent by this nation’s president from hauling government records out of Austin, in the so-called Archive War. That president had argued that Austin was too exposed to attack.
tossups.r: That president was Sam Houston. For 10 points, name this nation that existed from 1836 to 1845, before it joined the United States.

tossups.p: Interim president David Burnet signed the Treaties of Velasco [“veh-LAHS-koh”] on behalf of this nation, in which a captured general promised to pull his army back beyond the Rio Grande. That general’s government rejected the treaties and refused to recognize this nation’s independence.
tossups.r: That general, Santa Anna, had been captured after the Battle of San Jacinto. For 10 points, name this nation, led by Sam Houston, that existed from 1836 to 1845.

tossups.p: This nation claimed the Rio Grande as its southern and western border, but Mexico insisted that the boundary was the Nueces [“noo-AY-sis”] River, farther north. After the United States took over this nation’s claim, a clash in the land between those rivers helped start a war in 1846.
tossups.r: John Tyler signed the resolution to annex it just before leaving office. For 10 points, name this nation, once led by Sam Houston.

tossups.p: In the Compromise of 1850, the state formed from this former nation gave up its claims to land in present-day New Mexico in exchange for 10 million dollars to help pay off this nation’s old debts. This nation had printed paper money called “redbacks” that quickly lost most of its value.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this nation, led by presidents such as Sam Houston and Mirabeau Lamar, that existed from 1836 to 1845.

tossups.p: France became the first European country to recognize this nation, in 1839, and its diplomat Alphonse Dubois de Saligny [“sah-leen-YEE”] later had a legation built in this nation’s capital. Andrew Jackson had recognized this nation on his last full day as president, in March 1837.
tossups.r: Its capitals included Houston and Austin. For 10 points, name this nation, whose first elected president was Sam Houston.

tossups.p: In 1839, this nation replaced a flag showing one large gold star on a blue field, often named for David Burnet, with a new design. The new flag had a blue vertical stripe holding a single white star, next to horizontal white and red stripes.
tossups.r: That “Lone Star” flag later became a state flag. For 10 points, name this nation that joined the United States in 1845.

tossups.p: In this nation’s first national election, in September 1836, voters overwhelmingly approved seeking annexation, and Stephen F. Austin finished far behind in the race for president. The winner of that race was barred from serving two terms in a row, so Mirabeau Lamar succeeded him.
tossups.r: That winner, Sam Houston, later served a second term. For 10 points, name this nation that the United States annexed in 1845.

tossups.p: In 1841, an expedition of about 300 soldiers and merchants from this nation tried to take over the Santa Fe trade, but New Mexican forces captured them and sent them on a long march to Mexico City. This nation’s president, Mirabeau Lamar, had sent that expedition.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this nation, whose first elected president, Sam Houston, had won independence at San Jacinto.

tossups.p: Lorenzo de Zavala [“dee zuh-VAH-luh”], a politician born in Yucatán, Mexico, served as this nation’s first vice president on an interim basis in 1836. He had signed this nation’s declaration of independence at Washington-on-the-Brazos in March of that year.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this nation, whose flag had a single white star, that existed from 1836 to 1845.

tossups.p: This nation’s second president reversed his predecessor’s more peaceful policy toward Native nations, and in 1839 his army drove most of the Cherokee people out of its territory. That president had earlier served as vice president under his predecessor.
tossups.r: That president, Mirabeau Lamar, served between Sam Houston’s two terms. For 10 points, name this nation that existed from 1836 to 1845.

tossups.p: After the U.S. Senate rejected a treaty to annex this nation in 1844, Congress used a joint resolution, which needed only a simple majority in each house, to do the job instead. John Tyler signed that resolution just days before he left office in March 1845.
tossups.r: Later that year, its voters approved joining the Union. For 10 points, name this nation that became the 28th state in December 1845.

tossups.p: Brothers Augustus and John Allen founded a town on Buffalo Bayou in 1836 and named it for a general, hoping it would become this nation’s capital. Their plan worked, and that town served as this nation’s capital from 1837 to 1839.
tossups.r: That town was named for Sam Houston, this nation’s first elected president. For 10 points, name this nation that existed from 1836 to 1845.

tossups.p: This nation’s 1836 constitution protected slavery, so many Northerners opposed adding it to the United States, and Martin Van Buren turned down its request to join in 1837. James K. Polk won the presidency in 1844 partly by promising to bring this nation into the Union.
tossups.r: It became the 28th state in 1845. For 10 points, name this nation, led by Sam Houston, that broke away from Mexico in 1836.

clues.t: Independent nation from 1836 to 1845, after it broke away from Mexico

Its capitals included the new town of Houston (1837–1839) and Austin (from 1839)

Its last president, Anson Jones, lowered its flag in February 1846, declaring the nation “no more”

trap.title: Nation, war, or state?
trap.body: The Texas Revolution (1835–1836) was the war that created this nation, and the Alamo and San Jacinto were battles in it, so naming the war or a battle is wrong when the question asks for “this nation” or “this republic.” Other short-lived republics have their own answer lines, such as the Bear Flag Republic (California, 1846) and the Republic of West Florida (1810), which also flew a flag with a single white star. Saying just “Texas” earns only a prompt.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “this nation,” “this republic,” or “this country” with Sam Houston, Mirabeau Lamar, Anson Jones, the Archive War, or annexation wants the Republic of Texas. If you are prompted, add “Republic of.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Republic of Texas (or Texas Republic or Lone Star Republic; prompt on Texas)

topics.name: Savannah, Georgia
topics.kicker: Georgia’s oldest city, founded 1733 · End of Sherman’s March to the Sea
topics.briefing: In 1733, James Oglethorpe and a shipload of English colonists climbed a bluff above a river near the Atlantic and laid out Savannah, the first city in Georgia, around a grid of shady public squares, most of which still exist. Eli Whitney built his cotton gin at a plantation nearby, and in 1864 General William T. Sherman ended his March to the Sea here, offering the city to Abraham Lincoln as a “Christmas gift.” Juliette Gordon Low founded the Girl Scouts here in 1912.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: With help from the interpreter Mary Musgrove, this city’s founder made friends with Tomochichi [“TOH-moh-CHEE-chee”], the leader of the Yamacraw [“YAM-uh-kraw”] people, who allowed English colonists to settle on a bluff above a river. Tomochichi later sailed to London and met King George II.
tossups.r: That founder was James Oglethorpe. For 10 points, name this city founded in 1733, the first city in the colony of Georgia.

tossups.p: The bench scenes in the film _Forrest Gump_ were shot in this city’s Chippewa Square, one of 22 surviving public squares out of the 24 laid out as the city grew. Those squares follow the founder’s plan, in which each neighborhood, or ward, was built around a central square.
tossups.r: That plan was drawn up by James Oglethorpe. For 10 points, name this city on the Georgia coast, the colony’s first settlement.

tossups.p: In October 1779, the Polish cavalry officer Casimir Pulaski [“puh-LASS-kee”] was mortally wounded in a failed French and American attack on this British-held city. Volunteers from the French colony of Saint-Domingue [“san doh-MANG”], now Haiti, also fought in that siege.
tossups.r: The British held this city for most of the rest of the war. For 10 points, name this Georgia port founded by James Oglethorpe in 1733.

tossups.p: At Mulberry Grove, a plantation upriver from this city owned by Catharine Greene, the widow of General Nathanael Greene, a young Yale graduate built a machine in 1793 that pulled the seeds out of cotton. The plantation’s manager, Phineas Miller, became that inventor’s business partner.
tossups.r: That inventor was Eli Whitney. For 10 points, name this Georgia port city founded by James Oglethorpe.

tossups.p: In December 1864, Union soldiers stormed Fort McAllister, opening a supply line to the sea south of this city. Days later, Confederate general William Hardee pulled his troops out across the river into South Carolina, and Union troops marched in.
tossups.r: Their commander then offered this city to Abraham Lincoln as a “Christmas gift.” For 10 points, name this Georgia city where William T. Sherman ended his March to the Sea.

tossups.p: In January 1865, Secretary of War Edwin Stanton and a Union general met with a group of Black church leaders in this city, led by the Baptist minister Garrison Frazier. Days later, that general issued Special Field Orders No. 15 here, setting aside coastal land for freed families.
tossups.r: That general, William T. Sherman, had just ended his March to the Sea here. For 10 points, name this Georgia port.

tossups.p: In 1819, a ship named for this city left its port on May 22 and became the first steamship to cross the Atlantic Ocean, though it used its sails for most of the trip. That departure date is now celebrated as National Maritime Day.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Georgia port city, where Juliette Gordon Low founded the Girl Scouts in 1912.

tossups.p: In April 1862, Union rifled cannons fired from Tybee Island broke through the thick brick walls of Fort Pulaski, which guarded the river approach to this city. That success showed that old masonry forts could no longer stand up to modern artillery.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Georgia port, which William T. Sherman captured at the end of his March to the Sea.

tossups.p: In March 1861, Confederate Vice President Alexander Stephens gave his “Cornerstone Speech” in this city, saying that the new Confederacy rested on slavery. Before the Civil War, this city’s port shipped huge amounts of cotton grown across Georgia.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this city that William T. Sherman offered to Abraham Lincoln as a “Christmas gift” in 1864.

tossups.p: John Wesley, the founder of Methodism, served as a minister in this city in the 1730s, and George Whitefield [“WIT-feeld”] founded the Bethesda orphanage nearby in 1740. Jewish settlers arrived in this city only months after it was founded.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this city founded by James Oglethorpe, the first in the colony of Georgia.

tossups.p: The songwriter Johnny Mercer, who wrote the words to “Moon River,” and the author Flannery O’Connor were both born in this city. John Berendt’s 1994 nonfiction bestseller _Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil_ is set here.
tossups.r: Juliette Gordon Low founded the Girl Scouts here in 1912. For 10 points, name this Georgia city founded by James Oglethorpe.

tossups.p: In 1912, a woman inspired by Robert Baden-Powell gathered 18 girls in this city to form the first troop of a group first called the American Girl Guides, which took a new name the next year.
tossups.r: That woman, Juliette Gordon Low, founded the Girl Scouts. For 10 points, name this Georgia city, where James Oglethorpe’s colonists landed in 1733.

tossups.p: Every March, the fountain in this city’s Forsyth Park is dyed green before one of the largest St. Patrick’s Day parades in the United States. An art and design college founded here in 1978, known as SCAD, has restored many of this city’s historic buildings.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Georgia port city, where Sherman’s March to the Sea ended in 1864.

tossups.p: A ship named for this city, launched in 1959, became the world’s first nuclear-powered cargo and passenger ship. This city’s port, on the river that forms much of the border between Georgia and South Carolina, is one of the busiest container ports in the United States.
tossups.r: James Oglethorpe founded it in 1733. For 10 points, name this city, the oldest in Georgia.

tossups.p: The colony that began in this city was meant partly as a buffer between South Carolina and Spanish Florida, and its Trustees at first banned slavery there. This city’s founder had led a campaign in Parliament to improve conditions in debtors’ prisons.
tossups.r: That founder, James Oglethorpe, landed here in 1733. For 10 points, name this first city of the colony of Georgia.

Oglethorpe made peace with Tomochichi, leader of the Yamacraw, with help from interpreter Mary Musgrove; Tomochichi met King George II in London

A steamship named for it made the first Atlantic crossing partly by steam (1819); National Maritime Day (May 22) marks its departure

John Wesley, founder of Methodism, was a minister here in the 1730s; George Whitefield founded the Bethesda orphanage nearby (1740)

Setting of John Berendt’s nonfiction bestseller _Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil_ (1994)

trap.title: Which Georgia city?
trap.body: Sherman’s March to the Sea started in Atlanta, which his army captured in September 1864, and ended in Savannah in December 1864, so mixing up the two cities loses the tossup. “Georgia” alone is not enough when the question asks for a city. The Savannah River, Fort Pulaski, and Savannah, Tennessee (where Ulysses S. Grant had his headquarters when the Battle of Shiloh began), are different answers.
trap.fix: John Bell Hood, “Atlanta is ours,” and Sherman’s letter to Mayor Calhoun mean Atlanta; Fort McAllister, Hardee’s retreat, and the “Christmas gift” mean Savannah. Oglethorpe, Tomochichi, the squares, and the Girl Scouts also mean Savannah.
trap.line: Real answer line: Savannah, Georgia (do not accept “Georgia” alone)

topics.name: Secretary of War
topics.kicker: Cabinet officer in charge of the Army, 1789–1947 · First held by Henry Knox
topics.briefing: From 1789 until 1947, the Secretary of War ran the U.S. Army as one of the president’s original cabinet officers, and for the first nine years the job covered the Navy too. The first was Henry Knox, George Washington’s artillery chief; later holders included Jefferson Davis, Edwin Stanton, and future president William Howard Taft. In 1947, a new law turned the War Department into the Department of the Army and put all the armed forces under a single Secretary of Defense.
topics.answerHtml: Secretary of War (accept War Secretary or Secretary at War; prompt on Secretary or War Department; do not accept “Secretary of Defense” or “Secretary of State”)
reject: chairman of the joint chiefs of staff
chief of staff of the army

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1876, William Belknap resigned from this post just hours before the House voted to impeach him anyway over payments connected to a trading post at Fort Sill. The Senate later acquitted Belknap, partly because many senators said they could not convict an official who had already left office.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this cabinet post, first held by Henry Knox, whose holder ran the U.S. Army.

tossups.p: John C. Calhoun created the Bureau of Indian Affairs in 1824 while holding this post under James Monroe, since relations with Native nations were then handled by his department. That bureau moved to the new Department of the Interior in 1849.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this cabinet post, held by Henry Knox under George Washington, that ran the Army until 1947.

tossups.p: The Baltimore fort whose defense in 1814 inspired “The Star-Spangled Banner” was named for James McHenry, who held this post under George Washington and John Adams. Adams forced McHenry to resign in 1800 because he was more loyal to Alexander Hamilton.
tossups.r: The first holder of this post was Henry Knox. For 10 points, name this cabinet office that ran the Army until 1947.

tossups.p: Joel Poinsett [“POYN-set”], who brought home from Mexico a red-leaved plant that now carries his name, held this post under Martin Van Buren during the Second Seminole War. Lewis Cass held this post under Andrew Jackson while the Black Hawk War was fought.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this cabinet office that ran the U.S. Army, first held by Henry Knox.

tossups.p: In the 1850s, the holder of this office imported camels so the Army could test them for hauling supplies across the deserts of the Southwest. The man who held this office then, Jefferson Davis, later became president of the Confederacy.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this cabinet office that Davis held under Franklin Pierce, first held by Henry Knox.

tossups.p: In 1868, the holder of this post refused to leave and barricaded himself inside his office after President Andrew Johnson tried to replace him with Lorenzo Thomas. The House then impeached Johnson for violating the Tenure of Office Act, which was meant to protect that official.
tossups.r: That official was Edwin Stanton. For 10 points, name this cabinet office that ran the Army.

tossups.p: Henry Stimson, who held this office under both William Howard Taft and Franklin Roosevelt, oversaw the Manhattan Project during World War II and briefed Harry Truman about the atomic bomb after Roosevelt died. Stimson had also served as Herbert Hoover’s Secretary of State.
tossups.r: In 1947, this office was replaced by the Secretary of the Army, under a new Secretary of Defense. For 10 points, name this cabinet office.

tossups.p: Robert Todd Lincoln, the only one of Abraham Lincoln’s sons to live past his teens, held this office under James Garfield and Chester Arthur. Robert Lincoln was at the Washington train station in 1881 when Garfield was shot.
tossups.r: The first person to hold this office was Henry Knox. For 10 points, name this cabinet post that headed the Army.

tossups.p: After serving as the first civilian governor of the Philippines, William Howard Taft held this office under Theodore Roosevelt, who backed Taft to succeed him as president in 1908. In that job, Taft oversaw the building of the Panama Canal.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this cabinet post, replaced after 1947 by the Secretary of the Army and the Secretary of Defense.

tossups.p: John Armstrong resigned from this office after he was blamed for the American defeat at Bladensburg, which let the British burn Washington in 1814. Secretary of State James Monroe then took over this office’s duties too, holding both jobs at once.
tossups.r: This office oversaw the Army until 1947. For 10 points, name this cabinet post first held by Henry Knox.

tossups.p: Until Congress created the Department of the Navy in 1798, the holder of this office was in charge of building the first frigates of the U.S. Navy, including the USS _Constitution_. The first holder of this office had earlier hauled cannons from Fort Ticonderoga to Boston.
tossups.r: That man, Henry Knox, is the namesake of Fort Knox. For 10 points, name this cabinet office that ran the Army.

tossups.p: Newton Baker held this office during World War I and chose John J. Pershing to command the American Expeditionary Forces in France. In 1917, a blindfolded Baker drew the first number in the lottery for the military draft.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this cabinet post that ran the U.S. Army from 1789 to 1947.

tossups.p: Russell Alger was pushed out of this office in 1899 after critics blamed his department for spoiled canned beef, disease in army camps, and supply problems during the Spanish-American War. His successor, Elihu Root, reorganized the Army and founded the Army War College.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this cabinet post, which was replaced after 1947 by the Secretary of the Army.

tossups.p: Simon Cameron of Pennsylvania resigned from this office in January 1862 amid charges of corruption in army contracts, and Abraham Lincoln sent him to be minister to Russia. Lincoln replaced him with Edwin Stanton, who had been James Buchanan’s attorney general.
tossups.r: Stanton kept this job under Andrew Johnson. For 10 points, name this cabinet office that ran the Army during the Civil War.

tossups.p: Kenneth Royall held this office briefly before his job was renamed, making him the first holder of the new title. The same law created a new post overseeing all of the armed forces, first held by James Forrestal, who had been Secretary of the Navy.
tossups.r: That 1947 law turned this office into the Secretary of the Army, under the Secretary of Defense. For 10 points, name this cabinet office, first held by Henry Knox.

clues.t: First held by Henry Knox (1789–1794), George Washington’s artillery chief; Fort Knox is named for him
Cabinet officer who ran the U.S. Army, and the Navy too until 1798
In 1947, a new law turned it into the Secretary of the Army, under a new Secretary of Defense
One of George Washington’s four original cabinet posts, with State, Treasury, and Attorney General
Edwin Stanton held it under Lincoln and Andrew Johnson; Johnson’s attempt to remove him, despite the Tenure of Office Act, led to his impeachment (1868)
Jefferson Davis held it under Franklin Pierce (1853–1857) and brought camels to the Army
William Howard Taft held it under Theodore Roosevelt (1904–1908) after governing the Philippines; he oversaw the Panama Canal
John C. Calhoun held it under James Monroe and created the Bureau of Indian Affairs (1824)
Henry Stimson held it under Taft and again under Franklin Roosevelt and Truman; he oversaw the Manhattan Project
After John Armstrong resigned (1814), Secretary of State James Monroe held both jobs at once
Robert Todd Lincoln held it under James Garfield and Chester Arthur (1881–1885); he was at the train station when Garfield was shot
William Belknap resigned (1876) hours before the House impeached him over payments tied to a Fort Sill trading post; the Senate acquitted him
Fort McHenry is named for James McHenry, who held it under Washington and John Adams; Adams forced him out (1800)
Joel Poinsett, namesake of the poinsettia, held it under Martin Van Buren
Lewis Cass held it under Andrew Jackson during the Black Hawk War (1832)
Elihu Root reorganized the Army and founded the Army War College
Russell Alger was pushed out (1899) after spoiled canned beef, disease, and supply failures in the Spanish-American War
Newton Baker chose John J. Pershing to lead U.S. troops in World War I and drew the first number in the 1917 draft lottery
Simon Cameron resigned in 1862 amid corruption charges and became minister to Russia; Edwin Stanton replaced him
Kenneth Royall became the first Secretary of the Army when his title changed (1947); James Forrestal became the first Secretary of Defense
Before 1798, its department oversaw building the Navy’s first frigates, including the USS _Constitution_
Stanton barricaded himself in his office when Andrew Johnson named Lorenzo Thomas to replace him (1868)

trap.title: War, Army, or Defense?
trap.body: This office ran the Army from 1789 until 1947, when a new law turned it into the Secretary of the Army and placed all the armed forces under a new Secretary of Defense, so “Secretary of Defense” is not accepted. Under the Articles of Confederation, Henry Knox held the same job with the title “Secretary at War,” which is accepted. The Secretary of State, the Secretary of the Navy, and the Cabinet as a whole are separate answer lines too.
trap.fix: Clues from 1789 to 1947, like Henry Knox, Jefferson Davis, Edwin Stanton, William Howard Taft, and Henry Stimson, mean the Secretary of War. James Forrestal, Robert McNamara, the Pentagon after 1947, or Donald Rumsfeld mean the Secretary of Defense.
trap.line: Real answer line: Secretary of War (accept War Secretary or Secretary at War; prompt on Secretary or War Department; do not accept “Secretary of Defense” or “Secretary of State”)
